set.descent_text: The standard descent is NOT back to the Ruth Creek car — it's over the top and down the Fisher Chimneys to Lake Ann, a completely different trailhead. From the summit pyramid, downclimb and rappel the gully system on the pyramid's south side: climbers typically make 1–3 short rappels off natural anchors (slings on rock horns, occasionally pickets left in snow — don't count on finding a picket anchor still in place) on a single 60 m rope, which doubled through the anchor gives rappels of about 30 m, to drop through the soft or icy sections of the gully, though capable parties often downclimb the whole thing instead. This puts you on Hell's Highway, a ~60 m step of steep snow/alpine ice that accesses the Sulphide Glacier. Cross the Upper Curtis Glacier (watch for opening crevasses and weakening snow bridges by late summer) and downclimb Winnie's Slide, a short ice/snow step that some parties rappel (~30 m) when it's icy or the snow beneath is soft, to reach the top of the Fisher Chimneys. The Chimneys themselves (class 3–4) are generally downclimbed rather than rappelled. Continue down through the chimneys to Lake Ann and out the Lake Ann Trail to the Mount Baker Highway/Artist Point trailhead — roughly 13 miles of trail from where your car is parked at Ruth Creek, so plan a shuttle, hitch, or stashed bike. An alternative is to instead descend the Sulphide Glacier all the way down toward the Baker Lake/Shannon Ridge side — a non-technical glacier walk-off with no rappelling required — but that exits at yet another trailhead, again requiring a car shuttle. Ski parties sometimes reverse the Price Glacier itself (skiing the Price Headwall and the glacier's eastern lobe back to Price Lake), but that is a specialized, avalanche- and icefall-exposed line, not the climbers' descent.

set.beta: Grade II glacier route (easy snow), up to 40-45 degree snow. Route to summit via Winnies Slide (40-45 degree snow) or Fisher Chimneys junction. 3rd-4th class scrambling on the summit pyramid. Active Hanging Glacier avalanches. Bergschrunds, crevasses.

Its listed hazards are Hanging Glacier avalanches, large crevasses, rockfall at Hell's Highway, late-season schrund difficulties. The corrected beta keeps the stored Winnie's Slide/Fisher Chimneys routing and the avalanche, bergschrund and crevasse hazards, and replaces the ice/mixed, 50-degree-ice and headwall clauses with the sourced values.

set.beta: Grade: 4th class YDS, AI2-3 ice, M1b mixed, PG-13. Technical: 3,000 ft vertical gain over 5 pitches on the ridge itself. Hazards: Extremely loose and unstable rock (especially late season), bergschrunds, extensive crevassing, icefall terrain. Route: From the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead, cross Coleman and Roosevelt Glaciers northeastward, climb low-moderate snow ramps to ridge at ~7,500 ft, bypass Cockscomb Tower on left via steep snow, continue ridge to summit. Descent: Coleman-Deming Route (easy-moderate glacier). Required: Ice climbing competency, crevasse rescue skills, glacier travel experience, rock scrambling ability. Protection: Few ice screws/pickets, glacier gear essential. Best season: Spring or early summer (late season loose rock creates high hazard). First ascent: July 4, 1961 (Murley, Musser, Vielbig).
set.fa: Chuck Murley, John Musser, and Klindt Vielbig, July 4, 1961 (first complete ascent of the ridge)

set.beta: Two start variations exist: the original 1951 Route, which is faster but includes a 'scary' 5.7 pitch, and a 1957 variation that starts lower and adds roughly 500 ft of climbing on more logical terrain to avoid it. On the 1957 line, initial 4th-class terrain leads into dense vertical tree-root climbing, a slabby ~60-ft horizontal gully traverse (5.5) with minimal protection, and steep heather sections requiring careful, finger-pressing technique. On the right-hand (1957) rib, a roughly 700-ft crux section of higher-quality 5.6 rock climbing leads toward a bivy site beside the glacier, below the snow arete and glacier that lead to the summit.
set.overview: A parallel, marginally easier line to the Northeast Buttress up the same 5,000-ft face, first climbed in 1951 with a 1957 variation start; mostly unroped 3rd/4th-class climbing through a 'dangerous jungle gym' of vertical brush, with a sustained roughly 700-ft crux rock band on the 1957 variation's right-hand rib.

findings.claim: beta and overview describe the 1957 variation (the ~700-ft 5.6 rock band) as if it were the 1951 Route
findings.evidence: The detailed trip report behind this text climbed the 1957 start, and says the 1951 and 1957 lines almost meet at a snow bowl and then diverge: the 1951 takes the left of two ribs, the 1957 the more prominent right rib. Its 5.5 slabby-gully pitches, the tree climbing and the ~700-ft 5.6 crux band are all from that 1957 ascent. A second report confirms the 1957 line is the western NE Rib. The fix attributes those features to the 1957 line; the 1951/1957 start sentence is kept as stored.

set.overview: Bonanza Peak is the highest non-volcanic summit in Washington. This route is the Northeast Buttress, a serious, mostly-rock alpine line that gains Bonanza's true (9,516') summit directly, branching off the standard Mary Green Glacier approach at about 8,350 ft. Climbing in the 5.7 range (the V, 5.7/5.8 grade belongs to the full three-summit traverse it begins), the Northeast Buttress offers sustained, exposed ridge climbing on generally solid but lichen-covered rock, deep in the Glacier Peak Wilderness above Holden and Lake Chelan.

findings.evidence: The only account (the 2004 first-ascent note) grades 'the first ridge traverse of all three summits of Bonanza Peak' V 5.7/5.8; the Northeast Buttress was its first leg, climbed in a little under four hours from the 8,350 ft base, 'in the 5.7 range, with wild exposure'. Overview fixed in place; the grade column is proposed below.
